rules.statement: When a request fails because of a known condition in stored state that the caller can fix through the API, answer `409 Conflict` with an RFC 9457 `application/problem+json` problem that names the stored item to repair. Don't let the exception escape as a `500`, and don't answer `422`.
rules.why: A `500` tells the caller the server failed, when the condition is known and a write repairs it. `422` is wrong because the request content is fine and the stored state is not (RFC 9110 §15.5.10).
rules.check: Look for exceptions about unreadable or invalid stored data that escape as `500`, or are mapped to `422`, when the caller can fix them. Also look for 409 problems that don't name the scope or owner of the item to repair.

rules.statement: Map a cross-cutting exception to its HTTP answer in one endpoint filter installed on the root route group. Don't write a try/catch for it in each handler.
rules.why: Answers from separate handlers drift apart, and a handler added later forgets the catch. A filter on the root group also covers nested groups.
rules.check: Look for handlers that catch an exception type which a root-group endpoint filter already maps, or new per-handler try/catch blocks that turn one exception type into a problem response.

rules.statement: When you add a more specific exception for a case that code already throws as a base exception type, derive it from that base type, give it properties that identify the failing item, and keep the original exception as its inner exception.
rules.why: Existing `catch` blocks for the base type still catch it, and callers can name the failing item without parsing the message.
rules.check: Look for a new exception type that replaces a thrown base exception (such as `JsonException`) but doesn't derive from it, has no identifying properties, or drops the original exception.

rules.statement: Authorize the caller before you resolve or read stored state whose failure is reported in the response.
rules.why: Otherwise a caller who may not make the request learns details about the stored state from the error.
rules.check: Check whether settings or document resolution, or any other read whose failure reaches the response, runs before the authorization check in an endpoint.

rules.statement: When an error message or problem detail describes invalid configuration, name the setting and the rule it breaks, never the stored value.
rules.why: The answer should tell the caller what to replace without exposing anything the caller's normal view hides.
rules.check: Look for error messages, problem extensions or log text that include raw setting values from stored documents.

rules.statement: A write's validation refuses only the violations its own change introduces. A pre-existing unreadable or invalid stored item it meets gets logged as a warning and skipped, and the walk continues. The item the write replaces must not block that write.
rules.why: If an exception escapes the walk, one bad document fails every write, including the write that would repair it.
rules.check: Look for walks over stored items during a write that let a parse or validation exception escape, or that count a pre-existing bad item as a violation of the write.

rules.statement: Page an on-demand report over a collection that can grow without limit: return a normalized limit, a default and a maximum, plus a continuation token, and allow a page to be empty while the token is still set.
rules.why: The work of one request must not grow with the size of the collection.
rules.check: Look for report or list endpoints that compute over every item of a tenant or collection in one request, or that treat an empty page as the end of the results while the continuation token is still set.

rules.statement: Don't map a fixed route segment under a collection whose item route is `/{id}` (for example `/clients/incoherent` beside `/clients/{clientId}`). Put it at a sibling path instead.
rules.why: The fixed segment collides with the item route, which would answer it as an identifier.
rules.check: Look for new routes whose literal segment sits where an existing route has a `{id}` parameter.

rules.statement: Report a different kind of failure in its own field (for example a document error message). Don't encode it as a structured violation with empty names.
rules.why: A caller that reads the violation's names would find none.
rules.check: Look for violation or error records built with empty or placeholder fields to stand for a failure of another kind.

rules.statement: When a log and an API both report the same computed condition, have both use one shared component to compute it.
rules.why: Then the log and the API cannot disagree about what is affected.
rules.check: Look for logic duplicated between a background handler that logs a condition and an endpoint that lists it.
